query: A heist that goes wrong.
A murder mystery in a closed setting, like a snowed-in hotel.
Someone inherits an old house and discovers a family secret hidden in it.
A family gathers around a dying parent, and old secrets come out.
An unlikely friendship between a lonely old person and a young outsider.
Two people who can't stand each other get stuck together and have to cooperate to survive. I'd like it tense, but with some humour in how they bicker.
A psychological thriller where the main character can't trust their own memory and you're never sure who's lying. Ideally with a twist at the end.
A parent who walked out on their child years ago tries to reconnect before it's too late. Something about regret and second chances, without being too sentimental.

I'd love a story about a small, isolated community that hides something dark: an old crime, a strange tradition, something nobody talks about. A teenager or an outsider starts asking questions and slowly realises the adults are all in on it. I want it creepy and atmospheric, more slow-burn dread than gore, with a friendship or a bond at the centre. Young adult is fine, but I'd prefer something adults enjoy too.

I'm looking for a journey story where two people who barely know each other travel together after a death in the family, like a kid and a grandparent, or estranged siblings. At first they argue and get on each other's nerves, but along the way they open up and grow close. I want it tender and funny, about grief and family, with a strong sense of the places they pass through. Walking, driving or by boat, any of those works. Not a religious book, though.
Cosy, rainy-evening, cup-of-tea book.
Something light and funny, I need to laugh.
A dark, unsettling read that keeps me uneasy the whole time, but without gore or graphic violence.
Dreamy, melancholic and beautifully written, where not much happens and that's fine.
A page-turner with short chapters that I'll finish in one sitting on a long flight.
I want a book that feels like a long summer holiday by the sea: sunshine, salt, lazy afternoons, maybe a first love or old friends reuniting. Nothing heavy, just warm and nostalgic.
Something bleak and cold. Snowy wilderness, isolation, quiet desperation, people pushed to their limits by nature. I like it when the landscape feels like a character.
Whimsical and a bit absurd, like a fairy tale for grown-ups. Talking animals or odd magic are welcome, as long as there's something sad or wise underneath the silliness.

It's been a hard year and I want a book that makes me believe in people again. Not self-help dressed up as a novel, but a real story where kindness wins in small ways: neighbours helping each other, an unlikely friendship, a community coming together. I'd like some sadness in it so it doesn't feel fake, but it should leave me hopeful. Contemporary setting preferred, any country.

I'm in the mood for full gothic atmosphere: an old crumbling mansion on a cliff or a moor, candlelight, long corridors, a family with secrets, servants who know more than they say, maybe a ghost or maybe just madness. Victorian or early 20th century would be perfect. I've read the obvious classics, so lesser-known ones or modern novels written in that style are welcome. Romance is fine as long as it isn't the whole point.
Life on a fishing boat in the North Sea.
What it's like to be a monk.
Being an astronaut stranded alone on a space station: the loneliness and the problem-solving.
Growing up in a travelling circus in 1930s America, behind the scenes.
What it feels like to be the only deaf person in a hearing family.

I'd like to experience crossing the Atlantic on a sailing ship in the 1800s: the storms, the food going bad, the cramped quarters, the sailors' superstitions. Emigrants or crew, I just want to feel the voyage.

Put me in a field hospital during the First World War as a nurse. I want the exhaustion, the smell, the impossible choices and the friendships between the nurses, told by someone who's actually there.
What does it feel like to climb a Himalayan peak and nearly not come back? I want the altitude, the cold, the fear and the team dynamics. Ideally fiction, but it can be close to real events.

I've always wondered what it's like to live through a siege as an ordinary person, not a soldier. Food running out, queuing for water, hiding in cellars during shelling, still trying to go to work or school, falling in love anyway. Any war or city works: Sarajevo, Leningrad, or an invented one. I want to understand daily life and how people keep their humanity, from the inside rather than from history books.

Someone close to me is getting out of prison after a long sentence, and I want to understand what they're going through. A novel from the point of view of a man who spent fifteen or twenty years inside and now has to rebuild a life: smartphones, finding work, family who moved on, the habits that stay with you. I'd like it honest and not glamorised, and if part of it shows his years inside, that's good too.
Discover Nigerian culture through a novel.
A book about Inuit life in the Arctic.
A story set in ancient Rome that shows everyday life, not just emperors and battles.
A novel that teaches me about Japanese craftsmanship, tea ceremonies and the patience behind them.
Learn how beekeeping works through a story, since I'm thinking of getting bees.
I'm looking for a book that's make me discover the dutch culture through the eyes of an expat who settles in modern amsterdam (2020+) and learn the culture, meet with dutch etc..
I want to understand the Partition of India in 1947 through a family story. How did it feel for people who had to leave their homes overnight, on both sides of the new border?
Take me to 1920s Paris: the cafés, the artists and writers, the jazz clubs, the cheap rooms in Montparnasse. I'd like a novel, with real or invented characters, that makes the period come alive.

I'm fascinated by the Silk Road and want to discover it through a story rather than a history book. Something like a merchant or a young traveller crossing from China towards Persia or Constantinople, with caravans, oasis towns, markets, and different religions and languages along the way. Adventure is welcome, but what I really want is to come out knowing how people lived and traded along the route. Historical accuracy matters to me.

My family is Irish on my mother's side and I know almost nothing about why they left. I'd like a novel about the Great Famine of the 1840s and the emigration that followed: life in a village when the potatoes failed, the decision to leave, the coffin ships, arriving in Boston or New York with nothing. A multi-generational story following one family from Ireland to America would be ideal.
Books like Agatha Christie, set outside England.
Like The Hunger Games, but for adults.
I loved The Night Circus and I'm looking for something with the same magical, dreamlike atmosphere.
Something like Murakami: a lonely narrator, strange events, jazz, cats and wells.
Funny fantasy that pokes fun at society, like Terry Pratchett.
I just finished Pride and Prejudice for the third time. I'm looking for another witty romance with sharp dialogue and social comedy, classic or modern, but please not an Austen retelling.
I like how Kazuo Ishiguro writes: quiet narrators who slowly reveal what they lost or got wrong, so you only understand at the end. Which other authors write like that?
Gone Girl was the best thriller I've read: an unreliable narrator, a toxic marriage and a twist that changed everything. Give me something with that same feeling that I can't trust anyone.

As a kid I devoured Jules Verne: the submarines, the balloons, the journey to the centre of the earth, the mad inventors and the feeling that science could take you anywhere. I'd love to find that again as an adult, whether adventure classics I missed or modern novels in the same spirit. Steampunk is OK, but not if it's all about the look. Exploration, invention and a sense of wonder are what matter.

Little Women is my comfort book. I love the sisters, their different personalities, how they fight and support each other, and watching them grow up over the years. I'm looking for other warm family stories about sisters or siblings growing up, ideally over a long stretch of time, with both happy and sad moments. A historical setting is a plus, but a contemporary novel with the same warmth would be great too.
A morally grey antihero I'll root for anyway.
A lonely misfit who slowly finds friends.
A strong woman in her sixties or seventies as the main character, and please not a love story.
A child narrator who understands the adults around him better than they understand themselves.
Two best friends followed across fifty years of their lives, through all the ups and downs.
I'd like a story told from the villain's point of view, where at first you hate him and slowly start to understand, maybe even pity him. Fantasy or historical, either works.
A female scientist in the early 20th century fighting to be taken seriously by the men around her. I want her brilliant and stubborn, and I want to see the science, not only the struggle.
A quiet introvert who would rather stay home with books gets pushed into a big adventure. I relate to that kind of character and want to see someone like me become brave in their own way.

I'm looking for a novel about an immigrant father trying to hold his family together in a new country. He works two jobs and doesn't speak the language well, his kids grow up between two cultures and start to be ashamed of him, and his wife is homesick. I want it from his point of view, with dignity and humour, not just misery. Any origin and destination, contemporary or a few decades ago.

Something about an old man looking back on his whole life: the woman he didn't marry, the job he hated, the son he never understood, the war he doesn't talk about. Maybe he's in a care home, or on one last trip somewhere. I like slow, reflective books where past and present alternate and you slowly piece together who he really was. Bittersweet rather than depressing.
Short novel under 200 pages.
Something translated from Japanese.
flag: translation: the catalogue records most translations as written in English

query: A recent novel, published after 2015, that deals with climate change without being preachy.
A 19th-century classic that's still easy and enjoyable to read today.
A light beach read, nothing over 300 pages, and nothing sad please.
My niece is 12 and obsessed with dragons. I'd like to get her a fantasy novel at her reading level, ideally the first of a series, with a girl as the hero.
A Russian classic that isn't a 1,000-page brick. I want to try Russian literature, but War and Peace intimidates me, so something shorter as a first step.

query: A novel written in the 1960s by someone who lived through it, about the generation gap between post-war parents and their rebellious kids.

I'm going on a three-week trip with lots of trains and no Wi-Fi, and I want one big epic fantasy series to get completely lost in. Ideally finished, so I don't have to wait for the last book, with a rich world, political intrigue, lots of characters and a good magic system. I've already read The Lord of the Rings and A Song of Ice and Fire, so something else please. Adult rather than young adult.

I like Scandinavian crime, but I'm tired of the same grumpy male detective. I'm looking for a crime novel written by a woman, set in Sweden, Norway, Denmark or Iceland, ideally with a female investigator. Dark atmosphere and long winter nights are a plus, but I prefer psychological tension to very graphic violence. Something from the last twenty years.
